title: Best Company Brain Tools in 2026 Compared
summary: Glean, Guru, Dust, Sana, Notion AI, Moveworks, and Jinba Brain compared side by side: connectors, knowledge model, governance, and best-fit buyer for each.
body_markdown:
### Summary


- **The field:** seven platforms dominate 2026 company brain comparisons (Glean, Guru, Dust, Sana, Notion AI, Moveworks, and Jinba Brain), and each is built for a different buyer.
- **The key distinction:** most tools use RAG, which ranks document chunks by cosine similarity and can return a different answer to the same question on different days; ontology-validated records return one consistent, traceable answer, with deterministic retrieval reaching 90–95% accuracy versus typical RAG.
- **The governance shift:** whether knowledge is validated before it goes live is now a primary selection criterion, and the audit-trail question typically arrives about a quarter after adoption.
- **How to choose:** apply five criteria in order (guess versus validate, deployment model, governance, integrations and MCP support, implementation reality), then request a scoped proof of concept measured against the organisation's own operational questions.
- For banks, insurers, and other regulated enterprises that need auditable answers and on-premise deployment,[Jinba Brain](https://jinba.io/) stores ontology-validated records behind a mandatory human approval gate, with standard pilots running four to eight weeks.


Enterprise teams now talk openly about their "company brain", the shared knowledge layer that both employees and AI agents query for reliable, permission-aware answers. The appeal is straightforward: a single source of truth that knows what was decided in last Tuesday's meeting, what the product exception policy states, and what the current credit limit for a given client is.


The problem is picking one. The market is crowded, the category definitions vary widely, and the most useful distinction, how a tool handles knowledge quality, rarely appears in marketing copy.


This directory covers the seven platforms enterprise teams most commonly compare in 2026: Glean, Guru, Dust, Sana, Notion AI, Moveworks, and Jinba Brain. For each, it notes what the tool is, which systems it connects to, how it models knowledge, how it handles governance and permissions, and who it fits best.


## The core distinction: guessing versus validating


Most tools in this category use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). RAG retrieves relevant document chunks using cosine similarity (a vector similarity score) and passes those chunks to an LLM to generate an answer. The results are fast and broadly useful, but they carry a structural problem:[the same question can return different chunks on different days](https://jinba.io/blog/km-platforms-beyond-rag-finance) , producing variable answers. Vector similarity is a ranking signal, not a control plane.


For general knowledge discovery, that variability is acceptable. For any process where an answer needs to be auditable (a compliance question, a credit exposure figure, a regulatory commitment), it is not. As enterprise teams have found, the audit-trail question typically arrives about a quarter after adoption:[usage looks healthy, then the team cannot produce an auditable answer to a compliance question](https://certant.ai/blog/best-glean-alternatives-enterprise-knowledge) .


The alternative is ontology-validated knowledge records. Instead of indexing raw text, this approach extracts facts from source documents, validates them against a predefined industry schema, and stores them as structured linked records. Every answer is retrieved from a validated record, not generated from a retrieved chunk. The same question returns the same answer every time.


The[evaluation criteria buyers apply in 2026](https://bridgeapp.ai/resources/blog/most-popular-ai-knowledge-hubs-for-teams) include AI search accuracy with citations, integration coverage, automated content maintenance, data security, and deployment flexibility. Governance, specifically whether knowledge is validated before it goes live, has moved from a nice-to-have to a primary selection criterion.

## Tool-by-tool notes


**Glean** is the benchmark for enterprise search. Its connector library is the widest in the category, and for enterprises that simply want a single search bar across all their SaaS tools, it is frequently the default starting point. Its limitation is structural: as a RAG-based system, it retrieves and generates rather than validates and stores. That is sufficient for discovery but not for compliance-bound answers.


**Guru** takes a practical step toward quality control with its Cards, a curated, expert-verified layer that sits above the RAG retrieval. Teams manually verify the knowledge that matters most. The trade-off is maintenance overhead: the verified layer requires ongoing curation, and the long tail of less-critical knowledge remains subject to standard RAG variability.


**Dust** targets developers. It provides building blocks (retrieval infrastructure, data source connectors, assistant configuration) and lets technical teams define their own pipelines. The knowledge model is whatever the team builds. Governance and validation are implementation responsibilities, not platform defaults.


**Sana** applies the knowledge layer to learning and development rather than operational search. Its structure around courses and live sessions suits organisations where knowledge transfer is the primary goal, not agent-to-agent consistency or compliance audit.


**Notion AI** is the most tightly scoped tool in this comparison. It performs well for teams that have already made Notion their single source of documentation. Its retrieval is limited to the Notion workspace, which is a meaningful constraint for enterprises with knowledge spread across many systems.


**Moveworks** is purpose-built for IT and HR service automation. Its strength is understanding natural-language employee requests and routing or resolving them. It uses RAG to surface knowledge base articles, but its differentiated value is the automation layer, not the knowledge model itself.


## Jinba Brain: the validated knowledge layer


Jinba Brain occupies a different position in the stack: a[specialized, schema-defined, validated knowledge store](https://jinba.io/blog/km-platforms-beyond-rag-finance) for AI agents, not an enterprise search tool or a document indexer. It is the layer that ensures every agent answers from verified company-specific definitions rather than from guesses about what a retrieved document fragment probably means.


The mechanism is two learning loops, both with mandatory human gates.


The **Data Update Loop** ingests data from email, documents, meeting transcripts, CRM records, accounting systems, and Slack. A fine-tuned small extraction model (not a large general-purpose LLM, which keeps repeated extraction costs low) pulls candidate facts from that data and validates them against the relevant ontology schema. For banking data, that schema is FIBO (the EDM Council Financial Industry Business Ontology); for insurance, ACORD Information Model. An Evaluator checks each candidate for schema conformance, referenced ID validity, deduplication, and SHA-256 hash. A human reviewer then approves or rejects the proposed record. No record enters the knowledge store without that approval. Raw source data is kept unmodified on-prem; the pipeline reads it but never alters it.


The **Interaction Learning Loop** captures corrections that users make during live agent interactions. Those corrections refine the agent's Skills (reusable procedural playbooks), not the underlying validated records. The same human review gate applies. There are no automatic knowledge updates in either loop.


The practical result: the same question asked on different days returns the same answer, drawn from the same validated record, with a traceable source path and SHA-256 hash.[Deterministic, ontology-grounded retrieval reaches answer accuracy in the 90–95% range](https://jinba.io/blog/km-platforms-beyond-rag-finance) versus typical RAG.


A concrete illustration: a general-purpose LLM using RAG might produce three different answers to the question "What is our total credit exposure to Client X?" depending on which document chunks surface in a given retrieval pass. Jinba Brain produces one answer, because the calculation rules for "credit exposure" are encoded in the FIBO-aligned ontology schema and the relevant facts are validated records, not inferred fragments.


Jinba Brain also supports on-premise and air-gapped deployment, a hard requirement for banks that cannot route internal data through cloud AI infrastructure. Jinba (Carnot AI, Inc.) is a[YC-backed, SOC II compliant platform](https://jinba.io/) . Jinba Brain is currently in piloting. A standard pilot is scoped to one department,[runs four to eight weeks](https://jinba.io/blog/km-platforms-beyond-rag-finance) , and measures accuracy against the client's own real-world questions rather than generic benchmarks.


## How to choose


Enterprise teams switch away from knowledge tools primarily for reasons other than price: unverifiable answers, deployment models that rule out air-gapped or sovereign infrastructure, coverage gaps across the data estate, and implementation burden exceeding what the team anticipated. Evaluating against those four points before selection avoids a costly migration later.


Apply these criteria in order:


1. **Guess versus validate.** What is the tolerance for inconsistent or unauditable answers? General knowledge discovery can absorb occasional variability. Compliance-bound processes, regulated calculations, and agent-to-agent handoffs cannot. If the answer needs to be traceable to a source and consistent across runs, RAG is insufficient.
2. **Deployment model.** Does the organisation have a hard requirement for on-premise, air-gapped, or sovereign cloud deployment? This requirement is a constraint rather than a preference and rules out most cloud-native tools entirely.
3. **Governance model.** Does knowledge need to be validated before it enters the system, or is post-hoc stale-content flagging sufficient?[Stale content and permission drift are now standard checklist items in knowledge-hub RFPs](https://bridgeapp.ai/resources/blog/most-popular-ai-knowledge-hubs-for-teams) . The question is whether governance is a pre-live gate or a post-facto audit.
4. **Integrations and actionability.** Does the tool connect to the systems that actually hold the relevant data? Can it feed structured answers to AI agents, or does it only return documents to humans? The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the baseline plumbing for connecting knowledge layers to agents. Confirm whether the platform exposes MCP-compatible endpoints.
5. **Implementation reality.** The extraction and adoption work is the more difficult half of any knowledge system deployment. A vendor that scopes a bounded pilot, measures against real client questions, and defines accuracy criteria upfront de-risks selection more than a broad feature list does.


## Summary


The best company brain tools in 2026 serve different buyers at different points on the guess-validate spectrum.


For broad enterprise search across an existing SaaS estate, Glean offers the widest connector coverage. For customer-facing teams that need a mix of curated and retrieved knowledge, Guru's verified card layer adds meaningful quality control. For developer teams building custom agents, Dust provides the infrastructure building blocks. For learning and development, Sana structures knowledge into formal programmes. For Notion-centered organisations, Notion AI integrates directly into an existing workspace. For IT and HR automation, Moveworks handles service resolution at scale.


For regulated enterprises where the answer must be consistent, auditable, and validated before it is ever stored, and where the data cannot leave the building, Jinba Brain is the purpose-built option: an ontology-validated knowledge layer, with every answer traceable to a source path and hash. That distinction determines whether an AI agent gives a correct, traceable answer or a confident guess.


Enterprise teams evaluating any of these platforms should request a scoped proof of concept measured against their own operational questions. Generic benchmarks do not reveal where a knowledge model fails under the specific conditions of a given business.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is a company brain?


A company brain is the shared knowledge layer that employees and AI agents query for reliable, permission-aware answers about the business. It connects to the systems where knowledge already lives (documents, chat, CRM, ticketing, meeting transcripts) and resolves questions against that content while respecting each user's and each agent's access rights.


The term describes a function rather than a product category, which is why the tools sold against it look so different. Most implement it with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): retrieve relevant document chunks, pass them to a large language model, generate an answer. A smaller group implements it with ontology-validated knowledge records: extract facts from source data, validate them against an industry schema, store them as structured linked records, and retrieve answers from those records directly. The distinction matters most when the answer has to survive an audit.


### What is the best company brain tool in 2026?


The best tool depends on whether answers need to be auditable rather than on a feature count. Glean is the strongest general-purpose choice for broad search across a large SaaS estate. Guru suits customer-facing teams that need a mix of curated cards and retrieved knowledge. Dust fits developer teams building custom agents. Sana fits learning and development. Notion AI fits organisations already standardised on Notion. Moveworks fits IT and HR service automation at scale. Jinba Brain fits regulated enterprises that need consistent, validated, traceable answers alongside on-premise deployment.


Evaluate in that order: guess versus validate first, then deployment model, governance, integrations, and implementation reality. A tool that wins on connectors but fails on auditability is the wrong tool for a compliance-bound workflow, regardless of the quality of its demonstration.


### What is the difference between RAG and ontology-validated knowledge?


RAG retrieves document chunks by cosine similarity and asks an LLM to generate an answer from them. Ontology-validated knowledge extracts facts from source data, checks them against a predefined schema, and stores them as linked records that answers are retrieved from, with no generation from raw chunks. The practical difference is that RAG answers vary between runs while validated records return the same answer every time.


Validation operates as a gate rather than a filter. In Jinba Brain's pipeline, a fine-tuned extraction model pulls candidate facts from email, documents, meeting transcripts, CRM, accounting systems, and Slack; an Evaluator checks schema conformance, referenced ID validity, deduplication, and SHA-256 hash; a human reviewer then approves or rejects the record before it enters the store. Nothing goes live automatically.


### Why does RAG return different answers to the same question?


Because the chunks it retrieves change between runs. Similarity search ranks passages by vector proximity to the query, and that ranking shifts as content is added, re-indexed, or re-weighted, so a different subset of passages reaches the model and a different answer comes back. Vector similarity ranks passages; it is not a governance mechanism.


For general knowledge discovery this is an acceptable trade-off: the answers are usually relevant and always fast. For a compliance question, a credit exposure figure, or a regulatory commitment, "usually" is not a defensible position. This is typically why the audit-trail question arrives about a quarter after adoption, once usage looks healthy and someone needs to reproduce an answer.


### Which company brain tools support on-premise or air-gapped deployment?


Among the seven compared here, Jinba Brain is the one whose deployment model is designed for on-premise and air-gapped environments, with raw source data kept unmodified on-prem and the pipeline reading it without altering it. The other six are delivered as cloud services, so a hard sovereign or air-gapped requirement eliminates most of the field before any feature comparison begins.


Treat deployment as a constraint rather than a preference. Banks and insurers that cannot route internal data through external AI infrastructure cannot adopt a cloud-only knowledge layer at any price, which makes this the first filter to apply rather than the last.


### How do these platforms handle permissions and knowledge governance?


Most inherit permissions from the source systems and add controls after the fact: stale-content flagging, expert verification workflows, usage analytics, role-based access. A smaller group gates knowledge before it goes live, requiring human approval before a record enters the store.


Glean inherits source-system permissions and layers search analytics on top. Guru adds role-based permissions plus expert verification of its Cards. Notion AI relies on Notion's page- and database-level permissions. Moveworks integrates with enterprise identity providers. Jinba Brain applies a validation gate to every proposed record, RBAC for both users and agents, and an audit trail carrying the source path and SHA-256 hash for each record. The question to put in an RFP is whether governance is a pre-live gate or a post-facto audit.


### What are FIBO and ACORD, and why do they matter for regulated AI?


They are industry ontologies (formal schemas that define the entities, relationships, and rules of a domain), and they are what makes machine-readable validation possible. FIBO (the EDM Council Financial Industry Business Ontology) covers banking and financial markets; ACORD covers insurance.


Once a schema defines what a "credit limit" or a "policy exception" actually is, a candidate fact can be checked against it rather than trusted because it appeared in a document. That is how a knowledge layer returns one answer to "What is our total credit exposure to Client X?" instead of three, and why deterministic, ontology-grounded retrieval reaches answer accuracy in the 90–95% range versus typical RAG.


### How long does it take to implement a company brain platform?


A scoped pilot runs weeks, not quarters. Jinba Brain's standard pilot is scoped to one department and runs four to eight weeks, measured against the client's own real-world questions rather than generic benchmarks. Broader enterprise rollouts take longer, and the limiting factor is usually extraction and adoption work rather than installation.


That is why pilot design matters more than the feature list. A vendor that defines accuracy criteria upfront, scopes a bounded deployment, and measures against questions the team actually asks de-risks the decision. One that quotes generic benchmark scores does not tell you where the knowledge model fails under your specific conditions.


### How does Jinba Brain compare with Glean?


They solve different problems. Glean is an AI search platform that indexes across 100+ company apps and retrieves chunks for LLM-generated answers, the right choice when the goal is a single search bar across a large SaaS estate and occasional variability is acceptable. Jinba Brain is a validated knowledge layer for AI agents, storing ontology-checked records behind a human approval gate and returning the same answer to the same question every time.


In practice they sit at different layers. Glean answers human questions across existing tools; Jinba Brain supplies agents with facts that must be provably correct (credit limits, policy exceptions, regulatory commitments), each backed by a traceable source path and hash. Where the requirement is discovery, search suffices; where the requirement is an auditable answer, search is the wrong instrument.


### How much do enterprise knowledge platforms cost?


Pricing in this category is quote-based and typically scales with seats, connector count, and query volume, so published list prices are rare. The larger cost usually sits outside the licence: extraction, curation, integration, and the ongoing maintenance of whatever verified layer the platform requires.


Model total cost against the failure mode the purchase addresses. If inconsistent answers are merely inconvenient, an affordable search layer may be sufficient. If an unauditable answer is a compliance event, the licence fee is dwarfed by the cost of the answer being wrong, and the relevant comparison is the migration avoided later rather than the per-seat delta today. Request a scoped proof of concept with defined accuracy criteria before committing either way.
